name: Vesugen
lead: Vesugen is a synthetic tripeptide, Lys-Glu-Asp (KED, also called T-38), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group in St Petersburg and described as a vasoprotective peptide based on sequences found in vascular-tissue extracts [3][8]. It belongs to the family of Khavinson peptides, short synthetic peptides marketed as organ-specific bioregulators for healthy ageing [3][8].

In appearance and longevity circles it is discussed as a peptide for blood-vessel and capillary health, which proponents connect to skin quality, circulation and a younger-looking body over the long term. Those links are claimed rather than studied: the published literature concerns cell cultures and gene-expression experiments, and the patent that names the peptide describes an agent for increasing capillary resistance [3].

Published work is mostly in vitro. Vesugen was reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged endothelial and tissue cultures [1] and to limit lipid peroxidation of human lipoproteins [2], and a Russian-language report examined synthetic peptides in elderly patients with organic brain syndrome [5]. It is not an approved drug in the US or EU and is sold by some vendors as a research peptide.

angle.text: Users who take Khavinson-type peptides do so for long-term ageing support, and vesugen is the one framed around blood vessels and capillaries. The appearance benefit is a claimed downstream effect of healthier vasculature; no study has measured skin or other visible outcomes.

paras: Vladimir Khavinson (1946 to 2024) was a Russian gerontologist who directed the St Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology and worked for decades on peptide bioregulators, mainly as geroprotectors intended to slow ageing. Wikipedia reports that between 1973 and 2013 his team extracted more than 20 peptide complexes from organs and synthesized about 15 more, and that six peptide drugs, among them Thymalin, Epithalamin and Cortexin, were approved for medical use in the USSR and Russia [8]. Short synthetic peptides named on the page include Epitalon, Pinealon, Cartalax, Livagen and Vesugen [8].

Khavinson and colleagues claimed the peptides lack toxic or allergic effects and can slow ageing and lengthen lifespan. Wikipedia notes that much of the supporting literature consists of his own group's publications and patents and that the page contains no independent critical reception [8].
Vesugen is formed from L-lysine, L-glutamic acid and L-aspartic acid joined by standard peptide bonds. Its molecular formula is C15H26N4O8 and its molar mass is about 390 g/mol [3].

In aged tissue-specific and endothelial cell cultures, vesugen was reported to raise Ki-67 expression, with docking analysis suggesting interaction with the MKI67 promoter [1]. It was also reported to promote differentiation in aging cell cultures [6]. In vitro, vesugen and other short peptides lacked direct antioxidant activity but modified lipoprotein structure to limit lipid peroxidation and raised red-blood-cell membrane stability [2]. Another report describes short peptides' antihypoxic properties [7].

Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, additionally describes work in Alzheimer's disease mouse models, effects on skin fibroblast function and on genes involved in senescence and apoptosis [3]. These secondary claims were not independently verified here and come from Khavinson-group publications.

Grokipedia attributes vesugen to Khavinson's St Petersburg institute in the late 1990s and early 2000s, designed to mimic vasoprotective components of natural polypeptide complexes from cattle blood vessels [3]. The 2007 Russian patent RU 2295970, filed in 2006 with inventors including Khavinson, covers a peptide substance that increases capillary resistance [3].

No studies found specific to vesugen in controlled human trials. A Russian-language report on synthetic peptides in elderly patients with chronic polymorbidity and organic brain syndrome exists [5], but the results cannot be attributed to vesugen specifically. Related work consists of in vitro and animal studies [1][2][6][7].

card.summary: A Lys-Glu-Asp tripeptide (KED) from Khavinson's lab pitched for blood vessels; cell-culture data, one small Russian human report, no appearance link.
card.note: Research peptide; evidence is mostly in vitro and from one research network.

quick.overview:
Vesugen is a three-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as a vascular-protective agent.

Studies are mostly cell cultures. A Russian patent exists for a capillary-strengthening use, but no controlled human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: Reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged vascular cell cultures, apparently by interacting with its gene promoter in docking models [1]. Also reported to limit lipid peroxidation of lipoproteins in vitro [2].
quick.risks: No systematic human safety data; not an approved medicine.
